book: 133 - Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney

chapters.file: ch03 - Perry Mason and Philosophy The Case of the Awesome Attorney.md
ch07 - Perry Mason and Philosophy The Case of the Awesome Attorney.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Mason is beloved because he personifies the ideal of objective, discoverable truth: in a legal system run by fallible, sometimes crooked lawyers and jurists (O.J. Simpson, Robert Blake, Casey Anthony), Mason cuts through false accusations and frame jobs to vindicate the innocent, just as the Innocence Project and the Brian Banks story do in real life. It frames the whole volume by casting philosophers and Mason as fellow truth-seekers who believe an objective truth is 'out there' and that the law is a transcendent, unchanging thing beyond the reach of the people who muck it up, and closes with a tribute to Barbara Hale, TV's Della Street.

chapters.file: ch09 - 1. Is Perry Mason a Good Guy.md
chapters.relation: Muyskens asks whether Mason is genuinely good, noting his spotless record may be pure resultant luck: he never knows when he takes a case whether the client is innocent, as 'The Case of the Velvet Claws' shows when Eva Belter lies, tampers with the will, and even confesses to murder yet turns out to have missed. Using Kant's good will and Nagel's four types of moral luck (circumstantial, constitutive, resultant, causal), she argues outcomes alone cannot make Mason praiseworthy, then reads 'The Case of the Deadly Verdict' (his only loss, where he keeps investigating out of faith in Janice Barton) and 'The Case of the Terrified Typist' (where he engineers a mistrial for a guilty client) as proof that his commitment to justice, not his win record, is what makes him a good guy.

chapters.file: ch10 - 2. A Paragon of Righteous Virtue.md
chapters.relation: Allinson reads Gardner's novels, especially The Case of the Blonde Bonanza, as philosophy disguised as pulp: Mason acts from curiosity, compassion, and justice rather than utility, a 'pure Kantian or ancient Confucian' deontologist whose loyalty to clients ('erase ATTORNEY AT LAW from the door') functions as his own Categorical Imperative. The chapter's crux is the perjury dilemma of the Blonde Bonanza: Mrs. Winlock's offered false testimony would free Dianne Alder, which Mason twice refuses yet curses ('To hell with it'), showing that the plot's deus ex machina dissolves but never solves the ethical dilemma, while George Winlock's truth-telling-at-any-cost mirrors Kant's prohibition on lying even to the Gestapo. Socrates's better-to-suffer-evil, Plato's Meno reversal, Aristotle's rhetoric, Confucian and Hebrew filial piety in Dianne's character, and Rawls's justice as fairness all serve as lenses on Mason's virtues.

chapters.file: ch11 - 3. Perry Mason v. Saul Goodman.md
chapters.relation: Scalambrino compares Mason and Better Call Saul's Saul Goodman, who pull the same shady moves (Perry's evidence switching in 'The Case of the Crimson Kiss' and 'The Case of the Restless Redhead', Saul's fabricated 'pie sitting' videos) yet receive opposite moral verdicts. He frames this through natural law (Aquinas, Kant) versus legal positivism (Hobbes's command theory, Nietzsche's law as power), the audience's 'God's-eye' perspective, and the means/ends distinction, concluding provocatively that Perry's tampering is actually easier to justify from the positivist side, since he gambles on hunches without knowing his client is innocent, while the show's premises (he is already rich and famous, his clients always innocent) make the material conditions of Saul's lawyering moot for him.

chapters.file: ch12 - 4. The Case of the Other Renegade Refugee.md
chapters.relation: McCrossin reads 'The Case of the Renegade Refugee' (aired December 9, 1961, days before Eichmann's verdict) alongside the film Operation Eichmann and Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem as three competing pop-culture portrayals of the Nazi criminal: monstrous, repentant, and banal. The episode's 'other' refugee, Arthur Hennings/Max Kleinerman, whose Father Paul-inspired 'religious peace' lets him recant on the stand and save Mason's client Harlan Merrill (himself a Battle of the Bulge 'deserter' living a lie created by concussion), supplies what Arendt found absent in Eichmann: empathy and genuine acceptance of guilt, complicating her banality-of-evil picture. The whole is set against the Holocaust as the century's starkest form of the problem of why the innocent suffer while the wicked thrive, and closed with Hogan's Heroes' provocative reuse of the same actors four years later.

chapters.file: ch14 - 5. The Case of the Witless Witnesses.md
chapters.relation: Arp uses his own false memory of who pulled the plug at his teenage band's show, the Innocence Project's exoneration statistics (69% involving eyewitness misidentification), and Mason's signature discrediting of confident witnesses (the police chief's tire-track testimony in The Case of the Dubious Bridegroom) to argue eyewitness identification is the deadliest evidence in court. He reviews Loftus's finding that memory is a reconstruction with added information, the Dutch El Al crash study of imagined TV footage, Neisser's Challenger flashbulb-memory study, the Yerkes-Dodson law, and Morgan's high-stress military interrogation study, ending on the paradox that all other courtroom evidence ultimately depends on someone's equally fallible eyes.

chapters.file: ch15 - 6. The Facts Don’t Speak for Themselves.md
chapters.relation: Muyskens asks why Burger and Tragg's evidence keeps pointing at innocent people, answering with Hume's distinction between relations of ideas and matters of fact and the problem of induction: inferences from past experience are never guaranteed. In 'The Case of the Shapely Shadow' the prosecution's seven pieces of testimony against Janice Wainwright are reasonable but false, and only Mason, because he believes his client, presses to the water-records discovery that exposes Cole Troy; 'The Case of the Runaway Corpse' then shows Burger and Tragg settling on Myrna Davenport on flimsy, self-contradictory evidence and simply failing to investigate, while Mason withholds judgment, checks her account against documents and witnesses, and digs until justified true belief is achieved.

Jordan argues Mason's real superpower is logic rather than client selection or legal brilliance: since conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a unanimous jury, and since by the problem of induction (traced from Sextus Empiricus's regression arguments through Hume) no accumulation of probabilities yields deductive certainty, the prosecution can never conclusively prove guilt while Mason need only exploit that structural gap, as in The Case of the Howling Dog's cab-driver and document evidence and the TV movie Perry Mason Returns where Della is the accused. He illustrates with modus ponens examples about Della and Hamilton Burger, contrasting sound deductive arguments with merely strong inductive ones like predicting Mason's next win.

Becker and Taliaferro formalize Mason's method with Bayes's Theorem: Mason only takes clients he believes incapable of the crime, so his prior of zero guilt makes him an extreme Bayesian for whom any evidence leaves the posterior probability of guilt at 0%, while Burger and Tragg's guilt-favoring priors and their confusion of P(evidence|guilt) with P(guilt|evidence) doom their reasoning regardless of the facts. Mason's fabrications, the doctored cab receipt in 'The Case of the Nervous Accomplice', the grooved revolver in 'The Case of the Restless Redhead', and the substituted parrot in 'The Case of the Perjured Parrot', are analyzed as deliberate manipulations of the likelihood function that reshape the evidential landscape until the real killer confesses, with Mason's openness and dialogue contrasting with the police's closed priors.

chapters.file: ch18 - III. Who Is Perry Mason.md

chapters.relation: Ketcham's tongue-in-cheek chapter 'cracks the Perry Mason Code': Mason's uncanny timing (rescuing Sally Fenner in 'The Case of the Negligent Nymph') is explained by making him God's messenger-angel of justice, classified through Maimonides' Mishneh Torah hierarchy of angels as a Malakim, the messenger who supposedly cornered Judas into returning the thirty pieces of silver after the Last Supper and later nudged Lincoln toward the Emancipation Proclamation and Machiavelli toward even-handed justice in The Prince. The half-serious payoff is a survey of real American cases in which courts rebuked lawyers and judges who imitated or invoked 'Perry Mason tactics', from the courtroom double-swap in United States v. Sabater to trial judges instructing juries 'This is not Perry Mason'.

chapters.file: ch20 - 10. Trust and Temptation at the Office.md
chapters.relation: Hooke counters the lone-wolf noir myth (Hammett's Sam Spade, suspicious of everyone) by reading the Mason stories around a triangle of implicit trust among Perry, Della, and Paul, who risk her arrest in The Case of the Silent Partner and his license for each other, a trust modeled on Alphonso Lingis's account of trust as 'a break, a cut made in the extending map of certainties'. He explores the perpetually unconsummated Perry-Della bond (the fake elopement and onion-tears honeymoon in The Case of the Caretaker's Cat, the goodnight kiss in The Case of the Daring Decoy), the secretary as bearer of secrets after Sissela Bok, the paradox of the detective who must conceal himself (Paul Drake's three bedside phones), and Mason's hierarchy of obligations topped by justice for underdog clients.

chapters.file: ch21 - 11. When Is a Lawyer Not a Lawyer.md
chapters.relation: Karavitis argues Mason is secretly two other professionals: a historian and a psychoanalyst. Following Plato's Theaetetus definition of knowledge as justified true belief and the correspondence and coherence theories of truth, he shows Mason iteratively reconstructing the recent past from facts to theory to revised theory, refusing Hamilton Burger's circumstantial first stories and hunting the motive that is history's 'why' (H. Stuart Hughes's psychohistorical method), exactly what historians do; then, via Freud's defense mechanisms, he reads the recurring courtroom confession as an 'abreaction' in which the murderer, confronted with lie and truth at once, breaks down on the stand, and Mason's own total absorption in murder cases (no private life in 271 episodes) as sublimation of something repressed.

Birondo evaluates Della Street through moral psychology and Aristotelian virtue ethics: she is an excellent secretary in the role-specific sense (the Gregg shorthand that traps Robert Caddo's contradiction outside The Lonely Heiress crime scene) and supplies the 'woman's angle' the office needs, while Perry displays Aristotle's practical wisdom in court but a failure of recognition toward her, under-crediting her and kissing her for her 'feminine charms' upon her skullduggery in ways that today would be sexual harassment. The chapter also applies Aristotle on habituation through Mrs. Caddo's 'wildcat' tantrums hardening into character, and asks whether Della's team-playing beyond her duties is admirable, sad, or itself the product of mid-century sexism.

chapters.file: ch24 - 13. Perry Mason as Greek Tragedy.md
chapters.relation: McCracken reads the show's formula as Aristotelian tragedy from the Poetics: what satisfies us is not the whodunit (we could never deduce Lola in 'The Case of the Silent Partner' or poor Fred Calvert in 'The Case of the Daring Decoy') but the build-up and cathartic release of pity and fear through reversal and discovery, sealed by the guaranteed confession and the lighthearted epilogue that follows the commercial break. She uses Aristotle's plot requirements (beginning, middle, end; reversal; discovery; a hero slightly better than us) to explain why serialized shows like Twin Peaks or Lost fail where Mason's guest-star structure, with Perry, Della, and Paul as uninvolved 'hosts', lets an episodic series deliver complete tragic justice in one hour, even switching our sympathies to the confessing murderer.

Hooke argues the confession, not the evidence, is the TV show's enduring legacy and a pioneer of the modern confession spectacle (Oprah, Dr. Phil, Judge Judy, Jerry Springer): the murderer who lied all episode suddenly avows 'Yes, I did it!' before judge, jury, and millions. Using Foucault's Wrong-Doing, Truth-Telling lectures, he analyzes the confession's three components (public audience, drama, surprise), the epistemic puzzle that a proven liar's self-accusation is nonetheless accepted as true (as when the jealous wife of The Case of the Half-Wakened Wife, innocent in the novel, becomes the TV murderer through sheer dramatic remorse), and Foucault's claim that modern justice demands the criminal's own account, the 'veridiction' that anchors truth where Gardner's beloved forensics offers only objective facts.

Hooke uses Nietzsche, the 'pale criminal' of Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the 'valuating animal' of the Genealogy of Morals, to dissect our culture of judgment, in which judge, jury, spectators, and millions of readers assess the accused with an element of self-satisfaction (am I not better than the murderer?), even as Mason's plots ask us to imagine ourselves in the criminal's situation. Working through means/motive/opportunity in The Case of the Mischievous Doll (the client accused of killing her own disguised self) and The Case of the Angry Mourner (the telescope-wielding neighbors who missed the real killer husband), he ends with Mason's maxim that solving cases requires 'sympathy and tolerance for crime', seeing through others' eyes into the soul whose trace of madness Nietzsche says we cannot creep deep enough to find.

Christiansen frames justice as our culture's master narrative and tests it through two episodes. In 'The Case of the Substitute Face', Laura Houser's retroactive misidentification of her father going overboard and the fingerprint expert's error illustrate Levinas's face of the Other as first philosophy: the face-to-face call to care and responsibility that Mason answers every time he takes on a client, including the guilty. In 'The Case of the Perjured Parrot', the parrot Casanova's testimony and the imposter-parrot trick let Derrida's deconstruction (meaning by difference, endlessly deferred) and Arendt's public-space dialogue expose how little proof witness testimony really carries, with Heidegger's care-structured Dasein and Aristotle's action-over-character view framing the closing questions about faces and witnesses.

chapters.file: ch29 - The Perry Mason Novels and Novelettes.md

holes.name: Legal Positivism (law as posited command)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-law view that law's authority comes from being posited or commanded by a recognized power, with no necessary connection to morality.
holes.why: Chapter 11's entire comparison of Mason and Saul Goodman hinges on the natural law versus legal positivism contrast, and only the natural-law half has a taxonomy slug.

holes.name: Reconstructive Memory (Loftus and eyewitness unreliability)
holes.what: The research finding that remembering rebuilds events with added information rather than replaying recordings, making eyewitness testimony systematically unreliable.
holes.why: Chapter 14 is built entirely on Loftus's memory research, flashbulb memories, and stress effects to undermine courtroom eyewitness identification, and no taxonomy concept covers the epistemology of memory or testimony.

holes.name: Bayes's Theorem (conditional probability and evidence)
holes.what: The rule for transforming the probability of evidence given a hypothesis into the probability of the hypothesis given the evidence, via priors and likelihoods.
holes.why: Chapter 17 uses Bayes's Theorem as its sole analytical tool, modeling Mason's and the prosecution's reasoning over guilt and evidence in priors, likelihoods, and posteriors.

holes.name: Alphonso Lingis
holes.what: American existential phenomenologist whose book Trust describes trust as a non-contractual break in the map of certainties and probabilities.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its account of the Perry-Della-Paul collaboration directly on Lingis's Trust, and the taxonomy has no entry for him.

holes.name: Catharsis and the Poetics of Tragedy
holes.what: Aristotle's account in the Poetics of how tragedy builds and releases pity and fear through plot, reversal, discovery, and characters slightly better than the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 24 reads the whole Perry Mason formula as Aristotelian tragedy with the courtroom confession as the cathartic climax, but the taxonomy's Aristotle concepts stop at ethics and metaphysics.

holes.name: Confession, Avowal and Veridiction (technologies of the self)
holes.what: Foucault's account of how the demand to tell the truth about oneself became central to law, penance, psychiatry, and the modern drama of criminal justice.
holes.why: Chapter 25 interprets the Mason confession scene through Wrong-Doing, Truth-Telling as a judicial drama of avowal and veridiction, and the taxonomy's Foucault slugs cover only surveillance, power/knowledge, and discipline.
